strengths: Practically significant problem: as DiT acceleration advances, VAE decoding becomes a real bottleneck (well supported by the latency breakdown in Table 9: 2.3% → ~32-41% after DiT acceleration), and the plug-and-play constraint (no DiT fine-tuning) makes the contribution immediately usable.

The paper is grounded in diagnostic analysis rather than blind engineering: SVD variance analysis motivates channel pruning (Fig. 4), block-wise latency profiling motivates operator replacement (Fig. 6), and progressive 3D→2D substitution experiments justify stage-wise replacement (Fig. 7).

Comprehensive evaluation: two backbone VAEs (Wan 2.1, LTX-Video), two hardware targets (consumer GPU and Jetson edge device), reconstruction metrics (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS), temporal consistency (warping error), end-to-end generation integration (Self Forcing, FastVideo, Causal Forcing) with VBench-2.0, high-resolution generalization on DAVIS 720p, and parameter/VRAM analysis.

Thorough ablations covering pruning methods (vs. random/L1), pruning ratios, distillation variants, and projection-layer initialization (Tables 3-5), with the W-matrix initialization trick showing a clear 6.25% quality improvement.

Honest limitations section (Appendix B.9) identifying failure modes (fast-moving tiny objects, dense faces) and an explicit discussion of architectural generalization (B.4-B.5), plus code availability supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the components are assembled from well-known techniques — least-squares linear reconstruction pruning (essentially ThiNet-style, explicitly cited), depthwise separable convolutions (MobileNet), 2D conv substitution, and standard feature distillation. The main novelty is the empirical recipe and the R²-based greedy selection, which is incremental for an ICML main-track paper.

The central analysis is loosely connected to the method: the SVD result shows the feature map is low-rank across channels, but the proposed method uses greedy R²-based channel subset selection, not an SVD-based projection. The gap between '22% of singular values explain 99% variance' and 'greedily keep 12.5-25% channels with a learned W' is not formally bridged; the pruning ratio choices appear heuristic per model.

Some claims are overstated relative to evidence: 'preserves full alignment with the original latent distribution' is only supported by an empirical t-SNE-like visualization (Fig. 10) and VBench agreement, not by any distributional guarantee; the '96.9% performance' framing is a non-standard and somewhat opaque metric. Absolute quality loss is non-trivial (Wan 2.1: PSNR 40.40→37.61, LPIPS 0.0190→0.0285).

Several presentation and rigor issues: apparent typos in Equation 2 (the denominator should be ||Y − Ȳ||²), typographical errors ('A5880' GPUs, 'Self Foring', 'ration'), VBench results shown only as radar charts without numeric tables in the main text, and no variance/seed reporting.

Baseline scope is narrow: only two structural-acceleration baselines (Turbo-VAED, LightVAE); no comparison against quantization or operator-kernel-level optimizations, no FLOPs/energy figures, and the reason 1/8 pruning is optimal for Wan while 1/4 for LTX is given post hoc rather than predicted by the analysis.

Training details raise reproducibility questions: the hybrid 10K-sample dataset (half reconstructed VidGen videos, half GPT-4o-generated prompts through Wan) is small and its composition sensitivity is not ablated; 300 GPU-hours on unspecified-generation hardware is reported but hyperparameter sensitivity (the fixed α coefficients) is not explored.

strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important problem: as DiT acceleration matures, VAE decoding becomes the latency bottleneck (supported by the paper's own latency breakdown in Table 9, showing decoding rising from 2.3% to 31-41% of pipeline time).

The motivating analysis is concrete: the SVD study (Fig. 4) showing ~22% of components explain 99% of feature variance, and the block-wise latency breakdown (Fig. 6) isolating CausalConv3D, provide empirical grounding for the two design choices.

The topology-preserving shortcut injection (initializing 1x1 conv shortcuts with the least-squares mapping W) is a sensible and well-motivated solution to the residual-connectivity problem that naive pruning would create, and is backed by an ablation (Table 4, ~2 dB PSNR gain over random initialization).

Evaluation is broad: two backbones (Wan 2.1, LTX-Video), two hardware platforms including an edge device (Jetson Orin), reconstruction (Table 1), temporal consistency via warping error (Table 2), integration into two accelerated generation pipelines with VBench-2.0 (Fig. 9), high-resolution zero-shot generalization on DAVIS 2019 (Table 6), VRAM/parameter analysis (Table 7), and plug-and-play tests on a third pipeline (Table 8).

Ablations cover pruning method, pruning ratio, and distillation strategy (Tables 3-5, Fig. 11), and the appendix includes an honest limitations discussion (B.9) acknowledging failure cases on fast-moving tiny objects and dense faces.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: each component is a recombination of standard techniques - greedy linear-reconstruction channel selection is close to ThiNet-style pruning (which the authors cite), depthwise separable 3D convolutions are standard (MobileNet-era), and phase-wise feature distillation is conventional. The contribution is a system/engineering combination rather than a new method or new understanding.

The headline claims are somewhat inflated by framing: 'maintaining up to 96.9% of reconstruction performance' corresponds to a 2.8 dB PSNR drop (40.40 -> 37.61) on Wan 2.1, which is not negligible; 'preserves full alignment with the original latent distribution' is only demonstrated with a t-SNE-like visualization (Fig. 10) and selected VBench dimensions, not a rigorous distributional test.

Baseline coverage is thin: only two baselines (LightVAE, Turbo-VAED), and the comparison to LeanVAE / WF-VAE (cited lightweight VAEs) is missing; the strongest claims of SOTA are based on a narrow comparison set. Notably, LightVAE is cited only as an open-source project, making its provenance and tuning status unclear.

Several design choices appear hand-crafted rather than derived: the assignment of specific replacement operators to specific blocks (mid/up0/up1 -> 3D DW Conv, up2/up3 -> 2D conv) and the per-backbone pruning ratios are selected empirically per model, which weakens the 'universal acceleration framework' claim; the Fig. 7 justification is coarse-grained.

The greedy channel-selection criterion is computed on a small training set (10K samples, half synthetic generations); the paper does not analyze sensitivity of channel selection to the calibration data or whether the R2 threshold generalizes across content domains.

Missing VBench-2.0 aggregate numbers: generation quality is reported only as radar charts (Fig. 9) and selected dimensions (Table 8) rather than the full 18-dimension scores or an overall index, making quantitative verification difficult.

Reproducibility gaps: the code URL in the abstract is empty; the 'NVIDIA A5880' GPU is non-standard terminology; the SVD analysis setup (which layers, how many samples) is under-specified; and training details such as sequence scheduling of the three phases (iterations per phase) are not given.

Writing quality issues: the 'Impact Statement' is boilerplate, there are typos ('ration', 'Self Foring-Wan 1.3B'), and the per-dataset R2 statistic in Fig. 5 is hard to interpret without the corresponding layer identities.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: the paper convincingly demonstrates that VAE decoding becomes the dominant bottleneck (2.3% -> 29.6% of end-to-end latency) once DiT acceleration is applied, and the diagnostic analyses (SVD low-rank analysis in Fig. 4, block-wise CausalConv3D latency profiling in Fig. 6, progressive 2D-substitution study in Fig. 7) provide empirical grounding for the design choices rather than arbitrary heuristics.

Technically solid core method: the shift from pairwise channel similarity to linear-dependence-based pruning with an R^2 fidelity criterion, the least-squares-initialized 1x1 shortcut injection to preserve residual connectivity across blocks with different retained indices, and the stage-wise operator replacement are all reasonable and clearly described, with a sensible three-phase distillation schedule including a phase-2 gradient mask to protect pruned channels (Appendix A.3).

Comprehensive and multi-faceted evaluation: two backbones (Wan 2.1, LTX-Video), two hardware regimes (RTX 5090D and Jetson Orin edge device), reconstruction quality (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS), temporal consistency (warping error), end-to-end generation latency in two accelerated pipelines, VBench 2.0 radar results, zero-shot 720p generalization on DAVIS 2019 (Appendix B.1), parameter/VRAM analysis (Table 7), and thorough ablations (pruning method, pruning ratio, initialization, distillation strategy).

Practically significant results: ~6x decoder speedup with 37.61 dB PSNR (a 5 dB gain over LightVAE at the same speed), consistent superiority over Turbo-VAED on LTX in both speed and quality, and 27-36% end-to-end pipeline speedup; the appendix honestly discusses failure cases (fast tiny objects, dense faces) in B.9.

The plug-and-play property is well supported: Figure 10's distribution visualization, the Causal Forcing transfer experiment (Table 8), and the latency-breakdown study (Table 9) together substantiate the practical claim that the decoder can be swapped into frozen pipelines.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: each component is a recombination of established techniques - linear-dependence pruning is essentially ThiNet-style least-squares reconstruction (Luo et al., 2017), depthwise separable 3D convolutions are standard (Sandler et al., 2018), and feature distillation with phase-wise schedules is conventional. The contribution is a careful engineering synthesis applied to a specific bottleneck rather than a new principle, which limits the paper's reach as a main-track contribution.

The headline claim of 'preserves full alignment with the original latent distribution' is overclaimed relative to the evidence. Alignment is only demonstrated via a qualitative visualization (Figure 10) and downstream VBench curves; there is no quantitative distributional measure (e.g., latent MMD, FID of decoded latents, or statistical tests), no theoretical argument for why output/feature distillation guarantees distributional alignment, and no analysis of failure modes of alignment.

The '96.9% performance' and '93.1% of original quality' figures are reported without a precise definition (presumably a PSNR ratio), which makes the quality-retention claims hard to interpret; for Wan 2.1 the absolute PSNR drop is substantial (40.40 -> 37.61 dB) and LPIPS degrades 50% (0.0190 -> 0.0285), so 'negligible quality loss' language should be tempered.

Some internal inconsistencies: the abstract/claims cite 12.5%-25% channel retention while the SVD analysis motivates ~22%; Table 3 shows SSIM improving when pruning from 1 to 1/2 (0.9253 -> 0.9307) without explanation; there are typos ('Self Foring', '1/4 ration') and the code URL in the abstract is incomplete, weakening reproducibility as submitted.

The comparison set is narrow: only two structural-acceleration baselines (Turbo-VAED, LightVAE). No comparison against quantization or mixed-precision VAE decoder acceleration, no comparison against training lightweight VAEs from scratch paired with cheap latent adapters (a plausible alternative to full retraining), and the greedy channel-selection algorithm's cost and sensitivity are not analyzed.

Training uses only 10K samples, and the paper does not study sensitivity to dataset composition or scale; the generalization discussion for Hunyuan/CogVideoX (B.4) is analysis-only (SVD statistics and untrained operator swaps) rather than full distillation results, so the claimed universality of the 'Flash-VAED family' is only partially substantiated.

VBench 2.0 results are presented primarily as radar plots (Figure 9) without numeric tables or confidence intervals in the main text, making it difficult to judge the magnitude of quality drops per dimension; some dimensions in Figure 9b show visible deviations from the original decoder.
